title: India's Festive Season Split Its Scoreboard: Trade Up, Household Spending Down
excerpt: Traders forecast a record Rs 7 lakh crore season while a 67,000-household survey found planned spending down 6% — the distance between the two is the story of Diwali 2026.
body:
• India's festive season produced three different scoreboards: the economy grew 7.8% in April–June with consumption up 7.1%, traders forecast festive trade above Rs 7 lakh crore, and a 67,000-household survey found planned discretionary spending down 6% on last year.
  • Much of the gap is a comparison problem: last year's season was lifted by GST cuts, so 2026 looks weak against 2025 but strong against 2024 — Navratri vehicle retail fell 6.5% year on year yet rose 26.8% over two years.
  • Big-ticket buying took the strain: smartphone sales fell 16% in the first three days of the online sales and card spending dropped 12–15%, while premium phones and large TVs still sold.
  • For diaspora readers with money in Indian consumption stocks, the test comes next: traders' final tally, vehicle data, and the Reserve Bank of India's December 2–4 policy meeting.

India's festive season did not produce one consumer story this year. It produced three, and they point in different directions.

The National Statistics Office reported the economy grew 7.8% in April–June, with household consumption up 7.1%. The Confederation of All India Traders (CAIT) forecast festive trade of more than Rs 7 lakh crore between Navratri and Diwali, a rise of 15–18% on last year's roughly Rs 6.05 lakh crore. And LocalCircles, surveying more than 67,000 urban consumers across 307 districts, found households planning to spend about Rs 1.97 lakh crore on festive discretionary purchases — 6% less than last year. Each number is real. They are simply answering different questions: how fast the economy moves, how much trade passes through markets, and how a household budget feels.

The year the tax cut ran out

Part of the apparent weakness is arithmetic. The 2025 festive season was lifted by GST changes on September 22, 2025, which cut the levy on entry-level cars and two-wheelers from 28% to 18% and lowered prices on other consumer goods. This year had no comparable tailwind. The auto dealers' body FADA recorded Navratri vehicle retail 6.52% below Navratri 2025 but 26.76% above Navratri 2024; passenger vehicle retail overall was down nearly 22% on last year and more than 10% above 2024. A decline against a tax-boosted year is not the same thing as a decline in demand.

Where households actually held back

The caution was real in big-ticket categories. Inc42's roundup of the season's early data put online festive gross merchandise value at $7–8 billion for the first leg, October 8–18, on Redseer estimates, while Datum Intelligence estimated the first four days at Rs 29,800–30,900 crore — down 7–10% on the same period last year — with card spending down 12–15%. Counterpoint Research found smartphone sales fell 16% in the first three days of the big online sales, with entry-level devices under the most pressure, and The Economic Times reported festive discounts 35–40% lower than last year. Premium demand, by contrast, held up: Amazon reported premium Android smartphone sales up 70%, with televisions of 55 inches and above making up 65% of its TV sales.

Underneath the choices sits a tighter household budget. Retail inflation rose to 5.54% in September from 4.83% in August, with food inflation at 7.74%, and on October 7 the Reserve Bank of India raised its repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50% — its first increase since February 2023. LocalCircles found 57% of households planned to spend, at an average of nearly Rs 20,000, while 31% planned no discretionary festive spending at all; among those who did spend, about 83% expected to use savings at least in part. Its founder, Sachin Taparia, pointed to household earnings not rising as fast as prices. Gold told the same split story in a different aisle: the World Gold Council found Indians spent 50% more on gold in April–June while buying 6% less of it.

What to watch next

The season's verdict arrives in stages: CAIT's final festive tally and FADA's full festive-period vehicle data first, then October–December company earnings, which will show whether the trade bodies' optimism or the household survey's caution better described what reached the till. The RBI's next policy meeting, on December 2–4, will show whether borrowing costs rise further for the households who funded this Diwali partly from savings. The consumer did not disappear this festive season. The spending was rationed — later, smaller at the big-ticket end, and drawn more heavily from the cushion.
